utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness please come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we get to the witness, let's look at the exhibits if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: . Yes. Can I explain the position about the exhibits. The Chamber has, I think, four binders. They're in two categories. I will only be asking the witness to deal with the first category of exhibits in two binders and the two binders rather overstate the volume of material that he will be dealing with because, as you will see, there is one exhibit which is particularly large and we had to decide as to producing it in part or in whole, and it seemed that it would run the risk of unfairness to produce it only in part, although we'll only be looking at it in part. That's tab 16, document C2954. So in reality, the first two volumes or the two volumes of category A materials are not as daunting as they look, and they are the documents I will be asking the witness to deal with. The second category of material comes in two binders and is material I shall not be asking him to look at all but are exhibits that I will be asking him simply to authenticate. They're documents we forecast that it may be necessary for other witnesses to deal with, and although of course authentication is not something we typically go through in a very formal way dealing with document's authenticity only when they're challenged, it seemed desirable given his ability to authenticate so many documents that a simple exercise of authentication should be gone through. So they will be dealt with by a single question, "Have you gone through exhibits in those other volumes? Are they what they purport to be?" And then they can be put on one side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, those documents include the ones which we've already been handed in a small binder, small folder, rather, which were the exhibits from, I think, the transcript, attached to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I was simply proposing to go through the exhibits the binders that's we have, noting for cross-referral purposes, where necessary, that they've been also produced in the Dokmanovic case and transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, we have read the transcript which we've had, so there's no need to go over that in any great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will be as sparing as I can. There are a few background details, although some context is probably desirable. And the witness will be dealing with matters here in more detail and with a different focus than the way he was dealing with them in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And dealing with the timing issue, he will be here tomorrow too. He's available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. There was one other matter. Yesterday I asked for a map. We were discussing it. In Kosovo we had a very useful atlas. It may not be possible to replicate that, but it would be helpful to have a map of the entire area with the municipalities marked on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've put out a request several weeks or months ago for similar maps or atlases. If all else fails, I'll simply go and buy or have bought a series of road atlases because they will have a road index and village names won't have changed and town names won't have changed. But I know that the teams engaged on trying to see if we can find something more like the Kosovo atlases to help you and I'll report back as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness come in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the programme that I have received, this witness, that is to say the witness who was examined yesterday, the planned time for his examination-in-chief by the other side was recorded as 6 hours but he was examined for almost eight hours. This present witness, Stjepan Mesic the time plan for him was 10 hours. That's was what was written down. And now I can see that suddenly, quite precipitously this time has been shortened down to four hours, four and a half hours for the examination in chief, at most, which introduces a certain amount of chaos with regard to all this material and my cross-examination in view of the time that I was first to have been allotted, and I consider that practice of this kind is untenable. These four large binders were something that I received last night or, rather, at the close of business yesterday so that was the chance I had to look into all the documents, but I hear now all the documents were disclosed in advance. But I don't think that this is the proper way in which I should be expected to work. Of course I don't think that this is a big handicap for me in lieu of the fact that this next witness in all respects is a problematic one in view of his personal criminal control in the breakdown of Yugoslavia. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not hear to listen to your comments on the witness. Now, in relation to your comments about the procedure, let me deal with it in this way: First of all, as a matter of accuracy, the first witness was six hours, ten minutes by my note, in examination-in-chief, so that should be recorded. Secondly, if this witness can be taken more shortly in examination-in-chief, that is to be welcomed. Thirdly, these documents had been disclosed before, so you have had them before. You will also have the opportunity overnight looking at them again to see if there are any of them you want to ask any questions about. You will have the opportunity tomorrow of examining him. We've dealt earlier with the procedure whereby this witness has been interposed, so we have nothing to add to our rulings on those matters. Yes. Let us have the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have another question. It has nothing to do with this witness, Mr. May. May I please? Yesterday I received a new list and order, and although I understood that you would be providing these new lists with a time schedule as well, for example, after this witness Stjepan Mesic, somebody else was introduced last night, his name is Djuro Matovina, and he was on the list of witnesses in the 40th or 41st place, and you can check that out in that list, the list of witnesses for this year. And then right after the next two witnesses, Slavko Kucuk who was not on the list for this year nor was he in the list of witnesses provided in the course of the year. So with both these individuals, I would need to have the 125.000 pages available to me and for me to look through them all to find out about witness under number 40 and 41, and I'm sure you don't expect me to be able to get through all that material by the end of the year. I think that this kind of procedure and practice, and we've already discussed this, must be left behind once and for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the future witnesses in due course. Let's hear this witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd take a seat. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: I don't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, are you presently the president of the Republic of Croatia? Does your history which is a matter of public record reveal that you were Prime Minister of Croatia in 1990, a member of the HDZ party, first vice-president and then president of the SFRY's Presidency during the events we are concerned with, and speaker of the parliament between 1992 and 1994, leaving the HDZ party in 1994? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason for leaving the HDZ party in 1994, in a sentence, was what, please, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. You said quite rightly that after I had left the HDZ, I formed another party, the Croatian Independent Democrats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was it about the HDZ that led you to your leaving it? In a sentence.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: I did not agree with the policies that were being waged with respect to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I did not agree with the policy which had the wrong model of privatisation in view, and I asked for the functioning of a legal state on the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn to the topic of the change in status of the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina that happened in 1989 and thereafter, and we can deal with this, I think, quite shortly. The change in autonomous status of those two provinces, how was that achieved and in what way was that connected to this accused, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Vojvodina and Kosovo were autonomous provinces and they were constituent elements of the Federation, just like the six republics. Serbia for a long time was not satisfied with the status of the provinces. And after Slobodan Milosevic came to power, they started to breakdown the status of Vojvodina and Kosovo, and this was done. They went ahead with that, and the leadership was replaced in Vojvodina and Kosovo, and its status was changed as well. For both of them, that is. So except formally, they ceased to be constituent elements of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that the leadership of Vojvodina and Kosovo was changed, was that changed, and we can have the names if necessary, but was it changed by people more favourable towards the accused, less favourable towards the accused or independent of the accused?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: The job was done in such a way that meetings and rallies were organised, and this was called the Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution. That's what it was referred to as. So large rallies were held in Kosovo and in Serbian Vojvodina, later on in Montenegro as well, and they led up towards the change in the leadership which was in favour of autonomy. And then we -- this was replaced and the leadership that came out in favour of the constitution in 1974. A new leadership was brought in, and it was one that Slobodan Milosevic liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard already of the accused's rise to office and power at about this time. Can you just help us, though, with one matter? The speech at Gazimestan, what effect, if any, did that have on people like yourself and those to whom you were in contact?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: After the speech at Gazimestan which Slobodan Milosevic delivered, it was quite clear what the new leadership of Serbia wanted, and the possibility of an armed struggle was intimated as well. What was said was that everybody should prepare and make ready for waging a struggle, but he said that armed struggles were not excluded. And that was the first time that anybody in Yugoslavia had ever mentioned the possibility of a war option, that is to say, the possibility of actually going to war. And like many others, I came to realise that a restructuring of Yugoslavia was being prepared which would no longer be a federal one and which would no longer be the one prescribed by the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the setting of the times, that single phrase "That armed struggles were not to be excluded" did that have an effect on people's understanding of what lay ahead?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: That sentence actually mobilised the masses, the masses who supported the policy waged in this way towards the disappearance of Yugoslavia, because Yugoslavia, as a federation, can be envisaged and thought of as a chain, a chain in which the republics and provinces were the links linking up the chain. Now, if you do away with one of the links, the chain is no longer able to function. In other words, the Federation ceases to function. And this meant that they were moving towards the end of the kind of Yugoslavia that we had had up until then. Yugoslavia, and I have to explain this, had three integral factors or integrating factors. One was Tito. The second factor was the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and the third factor was the army. Tito had disappeared, the party had disappeared, and all that remained to be done was for the army to fall. So all this indicated the breakdown of the kind of Yugoslavia that had been established in 1974, that is to say, by the constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn from your observations about those events to your first encounter with the accused. In what year did that happen?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, I followed the development of the accused in his rise to power, which is to say from the eighth meeting of the Serbian Central Committee and then via the destruction of the Vojvodina and Kosovo and Montenegrin leadership. I followed his ascent right up to the time when I met him personally, which was when I personally arrived in Belgrade when I was elected to the Croatian Sabor Assembly as member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your first face-to-face meeting with him was where? Was it in the parliament? And if so, can you tell us -- wherever it was, can you tell us what was said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: After I was elected, after great pressure being exerted on Slobodan Milosevic to acquiesce and to agree with respect to me and Croatia taking its rightful place in the Presidency of Yugoslavia, let me say there was great pressure being exerted from the Serbian bloc in the Presidency by which Milosevic worked. The pressure was to exclude me, although the Croatian Sabor or Assembly had elected me, but they wanted to exclude me from the Presidency saying the Croatian Assembly could bring anybody else though chose to bring. Of course this was impossible because there were rules and regulations, rules of procedure and laws according to which this could not be changed. And there was great pressure from the international community which led to the fact that I was indeed elected. And then Milosevic called me up, called me into his cabinet together with President Tudjman, and that was where we had our first meeting and talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you remember of what he said on that occasion, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, there are two topics of discussion. One was Kosovo, the Kosovo issue, because we wondered how this problem was going to be solved because it was one that was a burden to the whole of Yugoslavia. Were we looking for a political solution? Milosevic said that we don't know the Albanians. We don't know what they're like. And he said, "When you give them a good slap on the face, then they'll be obedient, and that's how we'll solve that point." The second topic was that if Yugoslavia were to disappear, this would mean the return of the Muslims who had left and gone to Turkey and other countries, and that on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, about 500.000 people of this kind would return, and they would change the national composition, the ethnic composition of the country, and this, in his opinion, would be a great problem for all the countries of the then -- or the regions of the then-Yugoslavia. And to support this view, he provided a document, documents and reports, which were elaborated and compiled by the greatest demographic experts. I took a look at those documents, but my only comment to them was that I think that Turkey -- I said that Turkey has a sufficiently high growth rate, and it seemed to me improbable that 500.000 Turks and Muslims would return. But President Tudjman took all these documents with him and took them back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did President Tudjman appear to have approve of the contents of these reports or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: He didn't comment much. He read some passages out loud, read Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. through some others and took the documents to Zagreb. And when we met in Zagreb, when the leaders met in Zagreb, he took out all these documents and all he said was, "Here you have world experts and their views, and they stress that if Yugoslavia were to disappear, 500.000 Muslims who had previously left Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia, Montenegro, et cetera, and Sandzak, the Sandzak area, the part of the Sandzak which is in Serbia, that they would return." He did not give the document to anybody else to read. He did not say that this was compiled by the people who lived in Belgrade or, rather, that they were Serb experts. He said that they were world experts. So he lent that material a bit more importance by doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn now to the establishment of the SDS party in Croatia and the establishment of the Serbian autonomous districts. Can you please in a very short time, summarising as far as you can, how it was that those Serbian autonomous districts developed and the influence, if any, of the accused over the SDS party in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm quite certain that Milosevic didn't favour any kind of Yugoslavia that would be either federal or confederal. That was not what he wanted. What he was interested in was a Greater Serbia which would be created upon the ruins of the former Yugoslavia. And in that case, the Serbian national minority in Croatia was to play a role, and that is why rallies were held there as in Serbia. They were held in the municipalities where the majority of the population were Serbs. Let me just say at this juncture that as Prime Minister of the government of Croatia, when the first clashes arose with some of the leaders of those municipalities that I asked to have talks with all the presidents of the municipalities. It was six or seven municipalities, and I wanted to speak to all of them to clear up these misunderstandings. They agreed to meet me and to see what issues had to be solved, what the problems were that could be solved round the table, round the negotiating table, and not rallies, because you know, no problems can be solved out in the streets. All of them agreed to meet me except Milan Babic, who was the president of the municipality or, rather, the mayor of Knin. He was not present. And his secretary, the secretary of the municipality, I think his name was Knezevic, told me that Babic was in Belgrade, that he was seeing Milosevic, and that until Babic returned, he couldn't tell me anything. He couldn't say yes or no. But regardless of whether the meeting would be held in Plitvice, Zagreb, or anywhere else, he would come. Now, as the secretary did not phone me back for a few days, I called up the municipality of Knin once again. That same secretary answered the phone and he said that President Babic had arrived back from Belgrade, that he had forbade all municipality presidents to have any contacts or anything to do with me or the government, the Croatian government, and that a meeting was out of the question. I didn't talk to Babic personally, but that is what the secretary conveyed to me. So this was an overture, an introduction to rendering the decision on territorial autonomy for that part of the country with a predominantly Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Babic's position following his visit to Belgrade, was it ever explained one way or another who, if anybody else, lay behind his position?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, when on the 17th of August the so-called log revolution took place and the access roads were shut off in many municipalities, that is to say roads leading through Knin, it was quite clear that this was an attempt at secession, to break off a part of Croatia. The army lent its support to this attempt, and the attempt to do away with the logs by using the police force and to open up the communications and roads going through this vital region of Croatia was not successful because the army prevented it. However, when I went to Belgrade myself, that is to say when I was no longer Prime Minister, when that term of office ceased, I went to Belgrade to be vice-president of the Federal Presidency, I received information there from my staff, those who were loyal to me, otherwise they're all from Belgrade, but they told me that Babic and others were coming from Knin and that they would be having a meeting with Milosevic and Boro Jovic, members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia from Serbia. I told Boro Jovic that if the Croats from Serbia were to come, I would call him because he was their representative in the Presidency. But when somebody was coming from Croatia, I kindly asked him that he inform me because they were citizens of the Republic of Croatia. He agreed to do this, and that's how Babic and I found ourselves in the cabinet of Boro Jovic, in his office, and he just said that the two were tricking him and that there was no question of autonomy and that there was no question of the kind of republic that they wanted to see and that they had deceived him, that Milosevic and Boro Jovic had deceived him and that we could decide all these issues in Zagreb, that we could quite easily sit down to the negotiating table and see what the outstanding issues were. He laughed and said that he would have a state sooner or later. And I said to him -- my response was, "You're going to lose everything, and you're not even going to have an office of any kind, a surgery, let alone anything else."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're now going to turn to the one exhibit that's substantial and slightly difficult to handle. It's the only time I think we're going to turn to it in detail. It's at the end of volume one of your materials, and in the new tab formulation, which I hope you find helpful and which we're indebted to Ms. Dicklich and Mr. Reid, I think. It's tab 16, C294. What I ask is that the usher takes the Croatian version of that which she has already. Page numbers don't entirely match. The page numbers that the usher can find are at the top of the bundle, and so I'm going to ask her in due course to be making those pages available to the witness to look at. In fact, what I think I'll do is the following: If the usher could be good enough, first of all, to take that exhibit and lay it on the overhead projector, page 1 of it. Yes. Take the whole exhibit with you, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the exhibit should be given a number at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the entire bundle could be given its own number with tab numbers for identification of the individual exhibits, that might be helpful, and any tabs that aren't produced can be removed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 328.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we look at, then, tab 16, because that is what this exhibit is, of Exhibit 328, and we can look at the overhead projector, we don't need a translation for the time being, we can see, Mr. Mesic, that this was a meeting on the 12th of July of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and these, as we'll see when we look at the English translation, are its official minutes. Just looking at this part of the document, we can see the names of those attending and their positions at the time. Included were yourself as President, and then Vice-President Branko Kostic, and members of the Presidency and I use their surnames for speed, Tupurkovski, Jovic, Bogicevic, another Kostic, Jugoslav Kostic, and Bajramovic. And in addition to those people present, there was also the President of the Federal Parliament, Slobodan Gligorijevic; the Prime Minister, Ante Markovic; and the Federal Defence Minister, General Veljko Kadijevic; Foreign Minister, Budimir Loncar; Federal Ministry of the Interior, Petar Gracanin; assistant to the Federal Defence Minister, Admiral Brovet; Ambassador in the Federal Foreign Ministry, Zivojin Jazic; and General Secretary of the Presidency, whose name you'll see later, Anton Stari and others. That's the meeting for which these extensive minutes are a record; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I hope this isn't a change of plans that would inconvenience the usher. I think if the witness now has the entire stack of the Croatian version of this document, which would mean getting the balance from your desk, we can then display to those looking at the proceedings the English version, because I think Mr. Mesic will be able to find the appropriate pages in the Croatian version. So if you give him the balance of that and he can just have those. Just give him that underneath the pile he's got there already. Mr. Mesic, if you could just allow the usher to reconstitute the exhibit. If you could just hand those papers to the usher, please, just for a second. I think I'd better have a look at them just before we go on and make sure that -- can you bring me all of the papers, please. My mistake. Thank you. Thank you very much. Give those to him. If you've not got an English version -- right. Thank you very much. We now hand an English version to the usher, please. And if the usher would be good enough to put on the overhead projector pages -- page 69 in the English version. And Mr. Mesic, if you would be good enough, please, to go to page 82. We're going to see through these notes, amongst other things, how you were recording the history and position at that time. With RI on page 82 of this meeting and RI on page 68 and more particularly 69, did you speak at that meeting about the log revolution that had begun in Knin, and did you go on -- and we can see this really in the middle of the page on the screen: "I think it is perfectly obvious what was intended. Then in order to prevent inter-ethnic clashes, the army comes to separate the two sides." You were speaking here of Plitvice, I think. "Gentlemen," you said, "there are no two sides in Croatia. There is Croatian government and those who oppose that government. If we accept this basic fact, then we can resolve the problem on a principled basis. Let me say quite openly that we are witnessing Serbian imperialism, whose aim is to create a Greater Serbia on the rubble of this Yugoslavia. For this reason, Greater Serbian circles have no interest in protecting the Serbian people living in either Croatia or Bosnia or anywhere else. If that were the case, then we could look and see what it is in the Croatian constitution, see what is in the declaration on minorities, on the Serbs in Croatia and on minorities, because the Serbs are treated separately there." You went on to say: "Let us see if the Serbs have less rights than the Croats in Croatia. That would be protecting the Serbs in Croatia. But that is not what is sought. Gentlemen, what they want is territory. They want to grab Croatian territory and they to trick the army into doing it for them. This explains the mobilisations in Serbia and Montenegro and the deployment of tanks on the border. Serbian reservists come to garrisons in Croatia and tanks come to Beli Manastir and other borders and now they want to trick the army into doing the job. So we shall withdraw from Slovenia, but we will not allow observers in Croatia, and we will force Croatia to its knees. Gentlemen, this can be done, but only with a terrible war and rivers of blood. Croatia will never give a millimetre to Serbia. That should be clear, once and for all, and there can be no Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina. "Communication," you said, "is possible between the Serbs and Croats in Croatia, with observers if necessary, either international or Yugoslav." To save time I pass on the next page to the concluding paragraph of what you then said, at the top of the page. Just a little higher up. Thank you very much. "Here, it is stated," you said, "that the Serbian people are constantly terrorised." Speaking of what allegations were made. You went on to say, "Not a single example is given where the police have done anything to anyone because of their ethnicity." Dealing with Knin you said, "The police intervened in Knin, Obrovac and Benkovac only after armed groups of citizens occupied police stations and took away weapons. In Pakrac, a group of armed men captured 10 policemen, occupied the police station and declared it part of the SAO Krajina." Mr. Mesic, those were your words at this meeting. Were they a honest and contemporaneous account of what had been happening?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what happened, and this is what I said at the meeting of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn in the English version to page 74. And, Mr. Mesic, can you turn in the B/C/S version to page 88. Did you shortly after say this: "Well, in the crisis spots the JNA will continue to play its role by separating the warring sides and preventing the spread of inter-ethnic clashes. In other words, White Eagles, Dusan Silni and Bozur, you can all continue to come to Croatia because the army will protect you, because you are a warring partner, and so we are again to invade the Krajina." You concluded after those observations about the White Eagles and the others: "The army must withdraw to barracks and defend only the international borders of the state." Can you perhaps, Mr. Mesic, explain those words to us in just a little more detail?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: In the Presidency of Yugoslavia, I insisted that the army should return to the barracks and that it should not play a political role, that it should not be a political arbiter. Serbia, that is Slobodan Milosevic, however, wanted the army to ostensibly divide the two sides, but there were no two sides. It was those who were attacking and taking police stations who, as later became quite evident, were trying to establish the borders of a Greater Serbia running from Virovitica through Karlovac to Karlobag. If you look at all the acts of provocation that took place, they were actually setting up the borders of a Greater Serbia. This was obvious, but it was also obvious to the army what sort of job it was performing, because Milosevic said, "Let Slovenia go." We know why he said that, because there were no indigenous Serbs in Slovenia. He said, "Let Croatia also leave Yugoslavia but not those Serbs who want to remain in Croatia." The territory on which the Serbs lived was, according to him, to remain in Yugoslavia. So the Croats could leave but without the territory inhabited by Serbs. This territory was not inhabited only by Serbs, but they were the majority in those areas. This was a trick. This was meant to deceive international public Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. opinion, Yugoslav public opinion, but it was also meant to deceive the Serbs in Croatia. The Serbs in Croatia were needed only to ignite the fuse in order for the war to be transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina. And with regard to Croatia, whatever territory could be wrested from it would be joined to a Greater Serbia. The Serbs in Croatia were tricked because Milosevic had told them that all the Serbs would live together in a single state and that this was their right because they had the right to self-determination. He was deceiving the world because he was saying that he was fighting for Yugoslavia. However, he was doing everything to destroy it. The constitution of 1974 said that the republics were states, and it was republics that had the right to self-determination; that is, they had the right to stay in the Federation or to secede from if. This could not be resolved by force. The deception was that he promised the Serbs they would remain in a single state because, as he said, they had been living in a single state up to that point. However, this was a community on a confederal model where the republics were actually states.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn over now to page 89 in the English, pages 107 to 108, Mr. Mesic, in the Croatian version to where you turn again - and we can look at it shortly - to the withdrawal of the army and connection of that to those coming from else where in armed state. In the middle of the page and this is you still speaking, you said this: "I assure you that if the army withdraws to barracks, and if all those who came from else where return with their weapons to wherever they came from, if the Croatian authorities grant amnesty to all those who took part, there would be no problems and no crisis spots. If we continue like this, separating the warring sides as if there were two states in Croatia, one being the SAO Krajina, let me paraphrase," you said, "because I have it written down somewhere what Martic and Babic said." And then you quoted, "We have the full support of the Yugoslav People's Army, and we are both doing the same thing as it is defending Yugoslavia." You went on: "They were defending Yugoslavia, but they did not mention that they were destroying Croatia. Furthermore, they say that Serbia, that is, the authorities in Serbia, support Krajina with all their measures." Was that quotation attributed to Martic and Babic a correct attribution, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: This is correct. What they wanted was to provoke a conflict, then bring in the army which would separate the warring sides ostensibly, and then to set up a new border. This was their interest, and this is what was done. That is why at this meeting I said that if a republic asks for help, the other republics or the federal bodies should provide it. But no one could impose on Croatia solutions which would have to be solved by the police. The army cannot be used to solve these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look at the foot of the English page, page 89, we come to the next passage of yours, Mr. Mesic, and it may be that we will ask you -- I will in fact, ask you to read the last sentence yourself and ask the court interpreters to translate it for us. If you'd follow me, please, however, until the last sentence. You said this: "Support --" I'll give the context. Kadijevic had asked: "When did Babic say that?" You said: "Support SAO Krajina with all their means," in quotation marks, saying, "These are their words, not mine. They also say that the authorities in Serbia support them financially and by all other means. The authorities in Serbia should say, 'We have nothing to do with you. You have to solve the problems here, which is the only place where you can resolve them.'" And could you, please, Mr. Mesic, just read in Croatian the last sentence of that passage in order that any error of translation in the English transcript can be corrected. Could you read the last phrase, please, on page 108.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: "Therefore, Serbia --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: "Official Serbia is supporting SAO Krajina by all measures." Then Veljko Kadijevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simply the last sentence beginning "Ali, Ali mislim." Just read that sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: "But I think that this is like speaking to a deaf person. It was falling on deaf ears, because these arguments meant nothing to them because Milosevic was carrying out his plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will notice the different emphasis in that phrase than the phrase that is in the translation. Thank you. Can we turn from page 89 in the English right onto page 205, and could you, Mr. Mesic, be good enough to go to page 226. And here I'm going to ask you to comment on not just what you said but also on what Veljko Kadijevic said in this passage. He says: "That is a question that needs to be resolved now. It is a big question. "You are seriously wrong if you think that the matter will be resolved if the army is withdrawn now, and you can embark on 'settling' matters there. Then there would be a real bloodbath. Why do that? This way we will be able to find a solution by peaceful means." To which you responded: "Croatian territory is being seized." Kadijevic said: "It will not be seized." And there's a handwritten note in the margin saying: "What have you done to sort out Knin?" And then you said this: "It has already been seized and is being seized. Croatian villages are being burnt and cleansed. Territory is being seized." Kadijevic said: "Stipe, do you want war?" You said: "I am trying to prevent war." He said: "If you are so keen to prevent war, why do you not accept the decisions?" You replied: "I would have to give up part of Croatia." Do you have any comment on that beyond perhaps acknowledging that it sets the scene for the positions being taken?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is quite clear. The army came in after acts of provocation had been committed. The army took territory, and it was quite clear that official Serbia was paying those who went into action because -- well, this was done either by Serbia itself or through the army, because you could not imagine a terrorist group getting hold of tanks, getting hold of weapons that only the army had. So they were acting in concert, the army, Serbia, and the so-called Krajina, which was to perform that part of the job in establishing the borders -- the new borders of a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we turn from this topic in general, just a reminder. If we can show it on -- thank you to the usher for dealing with those papers. That's the end of that exercise Your Honours, that's the only exhibit exercise that's to be time-consuming. We can just remind ourselves by looking at document C341, which is tab 4 in the map binder. Notwithstanding your efforts, Mr. Mesic, does this map reveal the SAOs that were indeed declared by the Serbs even though they weren't able to take territory exactly identical to that of the areas they declared?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the area that they controlled. This was not all they wanted. They wanted more. But at that time, this was under the control of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next topic, and briefly. The role of the SDS party in Croatia. What role did the party take in general terms? What effects did its actions have on Serbs in Croatia, both radical and less radical Serb inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: At the beginning when the SDS was being set up, it did not appear that that party would become too radical. It was to struggle for cultural autonomy. But as time went on, it became evident that this party was being manipulated by Belgrade, which means the regime of Slobodan Milosevic and he himself, and that they were doing only things that would lead to the creation of a Greater Serbia, an ethnically pure territory cleansed of the non-Serbian population. In areas where the SDS took power, the population was completely cleansed, that is, is the non-Serbian population. This was an organisation that was to bring a dowry to Greater Serbia in the form of new territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to turn now to look in a little more detail at the Presidency of the Federal Republic, the SFRY. You've already told us in general terms about the change in composition that led to a Serbian bloc.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the names in paragraph 8 have, I think but I'm afraid I haven't checked, been given else where. They are in any event a matter of public record and I don't propose to take time by simply reading them into the record at the moment. They're there for consideration if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go to paragraph 9? In accordance with the constitutional system of a rotating Presidency where the President of the Presidency held office for one year, did Borisav Jovic take that office on the 15th of March of 1990 with you as vice-president?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He did take over that office. But I did not take over the office of vice-president immediately because the Federal Assembly kept putting it off for a few months. They did not meet for a few months so that I would assume that office as late as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as Borisav Jovic is concerned, to what degree could you assess did he act independently of anybody else or in cooperation with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Borisav Jovic did not have any independence whatsoever. Everything he did was done in agreement with Slobodan Milosevic. So even at the sessions of the Presidency I would often joke when a decision would have to be passed. Borisav Jovic would leave the session. He would excuse himself, and he would walk out of the room. I would always say, "Say hello to Milosevic." And when he came back, when he returned with his instructions as to how he should act, when he would take a certain position, then the members of the Serbian bloc would act accordingly. When he would return to the room, I would again say to him, "Did you say hello to Milosevic?" He did get a bit upset by it, but that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he ever challenge the suggestion that you were making that he was acting at the accused's instructions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. But my staff members told me that whenever he went out, he always called Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we move forward in time to the 12th of March of 1991, coming to the end of what would have been Jovic's year in office, and the consideration of the declaration of the state of emergency. What was the attitude of the Presidency members to this and of Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: It was quite clear that the top echelons of the army together with the Secretary for Defence, Veljko Kadijevic, had reached agreement with Milosevic or, rather, the Serbian leadership to go for a state of emergency. That meant that the army would be given the right to decide freely and that the army would decide where it would operate. At the session of the Presidency, this was not approved. The Serbian bloc got all worked up. Some of them resigned, Borisav Jovic among them, and the representative of Montenegro, Nenad Bucin. Milosevic sent a message via television that Yugoslavia ceased to function in this way, that they did not recognise any decisions made by the Presidency and that Serbia was to establish its own armed forces. That meant that Milosevic had announced a coup, that he announced that Serbia would no longer be loyal to the legally elected Presidency. That practically meant that they had opted for finally destroying Yugoslavia. Why this action was given up on is something that I cannot figure out until the present day. After this announcement, I spoke on television myself immediately, and I said that nothing special happened. Some members of the Presidency resigned. The republics whose representatives had left would simply have new candidates and would elect new members. As vice-president, I would assume my role and the Presidency would go on functioning. A few days later, Borisav Jovic came back as if nothing had happened, because the parliament purportedly did not accept his resignation, so we went on functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of things we can do to flesh out this story, Mr. Mesic. First of all, so far as Jovic's resignation is concerned and the resignation of others, is there anything leading to you believe that this was a spontaneous and genuine action or a planned action or are you unable to express a view?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: This could not have been a spontaneous act on his part at all. It could not have involved any kind of moral approach. He had simply carried out a task. It was obvious. When a state of emergency was not imposed, Milosevic said that there was no Yugoslavia and that Serbia had to take care of itself. So it was a scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second thing we can do is to look at the statement that the accused made on the 16th of March. This is the only other exhibit, as I say, Your Honour, that will take some time, but I think it's worth looking at in full. We have transcripts available of it. The witness has viewed it recently. Tab 29 in volume 2. And if the booth would be good enough, please, when we've all found our papers, to play the video. I'm grateful to the usher. That's -- tab 29, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In volume 2 of category 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's right at the end, Your Honour. Absolutely the last document. There might have been an easier way to help you find it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The last stage of its agony. The Presidency of the SFRY has not been functioning for a long time now and the illusion of the efforts made by the Presidency of Yugoslavia that are actually not to be is one that has been dead as of last night. This is not a step backwards. It's a step forwards because the truth is better than illusions and deceits. Yugoslavia lost its Presidency but it did not loose its workers, farmers, millions of its citizens, hard and honest workers who worked hard and to took care of their families. Millions of these honest and normal people will never give their country away. "As far as Serbia is concerned, it has always been in favour of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslavia, and it never concealed that. Absolutely convinced and proud Serbia publicly states this now as well. The blockade of the functions of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by those who are disintegrating the country had brought this plan into its final stage. This plan is being carried out to the detriment of the vital interests of the Serb people both in Serbia and in Yugoslavia instead of a democratic federation which is supposed to make it possible for the Serb people together with the other people to live on a footing of equality and together in one state. The forces of the anti-Serb coalition have formed and are now making every effort to disintegrate Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia does exist and it cannot be abolished by a one-sided act and a fait accompli policy because realistic interests, achieved freedoms, democratic institutions and the power of the people who live in it are guarantees of its survival and successful development. By directly sabotaging its own order on disarming paramilitary formations, the Presidency of the SFRY enabled the creation of republican armies that pose an immediate threat to the security of the country, all its citizens and especially the Republic of Serbia and the Serb people outside of Serbia. "The Presidency of Yugoslavia which is also the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, all the time since this order was passed, there was blockade of functions of the Yugoslav People's Army which is duty-bound and capable of protecting the people from war, regardless of whether it's a civil war or a war of conquest. The Presidency of the SFRY did everything in its power so that its own order would not be carried out and so the secession of certain republics and parts of Yugoslavia would be carried out by combining political manoeuvres, obstructions and armed conflicts instead of in a peaceful way by respecting the rights of all people to self-determination. "By resigning from the Presidency of Yugoslavia and the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, Dr. Borisav Jovic refused to accept the blockade and obstruction of the state leadership at a moment that was crucial for the country. I believe that the resignation of Borisav Jovic under the given circumstances represents an act of responsibility of a responsible man who does not wish to take part in the break-up of his country and it is an act of rebellion against obstruction in the state leadership. "In view of this situation, I wish to announce that the Republic of Serbia will not recognise a single decision reached by the SFRY Presidency because under existing circumstances, any such decision would be illegitimate. As for the operation of such a Presidency that opted for the disintegration of Yugoslavia, I personally will not accept any participation in terms of authority that would be conducive from the resignation of Borisav Jovic and would be vested in me personally. I expect that the Yugoslav and international public will understand that not a single patriot can accept the legitimacy of a collective head of state operating against his country and the valid constitution. I demand that the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, in accordance with the acts of the takeover of authority from the Kosovo Assembly reach a decision at its first session on the release of Riza Sapundziju from the office of member of the SFRY Presidency. Under existing circumstances attempts to set off violence in Sandzak, Kosovo and Metohija, I have ordered a mobilisation of reserve forces of the Republic of Serbia, MUP security forces and urgent establishment of additional police forces of the Republic of Serbia. I ask the government of the Republic of Serbia to carry out all preparations for the establishment of additional forces in a size that would guarantee the protection of the interests of the Republic of Serbia and the Serb people. I call upon all political parties in this difficult situation to establish full cooperation and also to disregard all their differences and mutual disputes in the interest of Serbia. I think that despite the newly created situation in Yugoslavia, there is no need to introduce a state of emergency. All institutions of the system and the life in the Republic of Serbia should continue normally. The citizens of Serbia should know that the Republic of Serbia is able to provide full protection of the interests of the Republic, all its citizens and the Serb people. "The Republic of Serbia, the citizens of Serbia and the Serb people will oppose all acts of disintegration of our country. Today we need to be strong and determined to defend our country as we have done so many times before. I'm convinced that the great freedom-loving spirit of the Serb people will triumph over forces of the anti-Serb coalition looming over Serbia and Yugoslavia that is our duty. Wisdom, courage and, above all, patriotism of the citizens of the Republic of Serbia and Yugoslavia are being tested now. As of this moment, we are taking that test. I believe in the victory of peace in Yugoslavia. I believe in the triumph of unity in Serbia and in the triumph of forces that will serenity to people, notably to mothers and to our children. "The Presidency --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the speed was extreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the interpreters for dealing with that, and I will --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the interpreters for being able to deal with that, and I will make sure that I move slowly over the next few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, there is a lot one could ask about that speech, but just a few questions to you about it. The setting is, as you've explained to us, that the Presidency had declined to declare a state of emergency which would have justified, in position of a state of war or something like that, had been the resignations and then this speech on television. I think you yourself spoke on television later although at the moment we haven't been able to retrieve the footage. Is that correct, you did speak?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see that the speech starts off by talking about the Federal Republic and the decisions that had been made or not made and about Jovic's resignation being justified, and then it turns to Serbia and deals specifically with Serbia and the Serbs. What is your comment on this speech? Was it a straightforward speech? Did it have any subtext that you could discern?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: It is quite clear that this did not mean saving Yugoslavia. It meant making operational the final dismemberment of Yugoslavia. In his speech, Milosevic says that Serbia no longer accepts the decisions of the Presidency. That is to say, that it does not accept the constitution of Yugoslavia, the SFRY. Also, he says that he would not accept the -- to be present in the Presidency of Yugoslavia, to act ex officio there, although he is duty-bound to do so if the members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia leaves. That means that when Borisav Jovic left, before a new member is elected by the Republic of Serbia, the president of the Republic of Serbia, according to regulations, has to be a member of the Presidency. He has to attend members -- meetings of the Presidency. But here he says that he is not going to carry out the constitution, the constitution of the SFRY and all the rest that he mentions, that forces would be mobilised. A threat was made to the rest of the Yugoslavia. In other words, he announced the disintegration of Yugoslavia. And what was this all about? I shall present it quite briefly. Slovenia and Croatia, assisted by Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia, we proposed to have a confederal system because the model of a federation as the one that existed was could not be sustained. That is what I always emphasised. The three cohesive factors were no longer there. And the only possible thing was a confederacy. However, until the present day, Serbia did not respond to our proposal to opt for a confederal solution, to reach an agreement on this, to come to a consensus and not act through the army and have solutions imposed on us. We could not accept Croatia, Slovenia and other republics to be treated the way Milosevic treated Vojvodina, Montenegro, and Kosovo. We could not accept that kind of federation, and that is precisely what he wanted, a firm federation. That is what I wish to say by way of an explanation. What was said was that confederations could not exist. They even said there was a confederacy in the United States of America. Well, true, but it did not fall apart. But it did function, and it -- and there is proof of that. It waged war for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other detail I haven't covered so far within paragraph 10 of the summary. When the Presidency declined to declare a state of emergency, what, if anything, did Kadijevic say about what the Serbs would do?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, at the session and what happened after that was that there were grave tensions. Objections were being made to Bogic Bogicevic, that he as a Serb, although he did not represent Serbia but Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he was not voting as a Serb and he answered that he was a Serb but that he was first and foremost a Bosnian and that he voted in the interest of his republic. So the situation was really difficult. And I expected Serbia or, rather, Milosevic, to make some even more heavy handed stepped, and indeed he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in particular, did Kadijevic say anything material to the Serbs' plans and anything about a Serb army?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Right at this moment, I cannot recall his words, but they were quite in accordance with what Borisav Jovic had been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look now, then, at an exhibit from the same period of time. It's in volume I of part 1 and indeed all the references are to part 1 of the document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit 328 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. 328. And it's tab 15, Exhibit number 2935. And if we look at this, if you'd have the Croatian or B/C/S version, Mr. Mesic, and if the usher could on this occasion put the front page on the overhead projector. You will see that this is a document from March 1991 coming from the Secretary Anton Stari at the bottom, coming to you in your position still as Vice-President of the Presidency. Just you in that position. Enclosing a text of a statement by the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces for your information. And then the next page, please, comes from or purports to come from the Supreme Command Staff and says: "Enclosed find a statement by the Supreme Command Staff," which is the result, and I'm going to skim read it, "Result of a comprehensive evaluation of the situation arising from the decision of the SFRJ Presidency not to accept the measures proposed." It goes on to suggest those measures would prevent interethnic armed conflicts. Next paragraph. "When opting for the conditions measures presented in the statement, it was borne in mind that the non-acceptance of the proposal does not absolve the armed forces and Supreme Command Staff, as an expert and professional body in the area of command and control, of responsibility for the country's survival and security, which are their constitutional duties and responsibilities and must be carried out unconditionally." Then says: "The Supreme Command Staff maintains that this should be pointed out publicly." It says: "The combat readiness of some of the People's Army units will be raised only depending on how the situation develops." And over the page, please, just the second paragraph of the statement itself. It says: "The Yugoslav People's Army will steadfastly guard the borders from all danger and will not allow them to be changed until an agreement is reached and implemented in accordance with the Constitution." First of all, your comment on this body, the Supreme Command Staff, and then secondly your comment on the document itself, Mr. Mesic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff is actually an illegal institution because the Supreme Command Staff could only be established in times of war or in a situation of an immediate threat of war. Since neither was the case in Yugoslavia, the Supreme Command Staff could not be activated. Throughout my work in the Presidency, I never managed to find out who the members of this Supreme Command Staff were, but it is obvious that the army says that it's going to raise combat readiness on the part of the units and that this will be done exclusively in accordance with the development of the situation. That is to say that they are going to decide on their own where the army is going to act. According to the constitution, they had no right to do so. So this is actually a military coup, not work on the basis of the Yugoslav constitution that was still in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a convenient moment. Mr. Nice, you're on course, I take it, to finish at least this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The balance of the evidence will move more swiftly because the exhibits will not take so long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mesic, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you please remember, and I must warn you as I warn all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over and that does include the members, of course, of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, following the resignation and reinstatement, as it were, of Mr. Jovic, you say there were two members of the Presidency who were replaced. Were the two who were replaced those who had been supportive of Jovic or against him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I didn't hear your entire question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies. Following the resignation and return of Jovic, you tell us that two members of the Presidency were replaced. Were those who were replaced or had those who were replaced been supportive of Jovic or against him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: One was replaced, and that was Riza Sapunzhiu, the representative Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of Kosovo. And Nenad Bucin tendered his resignation. He was the representative of Montenegro. Riza Sapunzhiu thought he wouldn't be able to be replaced by anybody because he was the Kosovo representative, and the Kosovo Assembly was the one which Milosevic had disbanded. So he counted on being able to vote according to his conscience. However, Milosevic ordered, as could be seen from the excerpts shown, ordered the Serb Assembly to replace Riza Sapunzhiu and this was carried out. In the Yugoslav Presidency, Sejdo Bajramovic was sent there, somebody whom nobody had elected in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At about this time in 1991, just really yes or no if you can to save time to this, about this time were some organs of the Presidency, such bodies as the military department or the council for the protection of constitutional order, functioning normally?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were functioning normally as far as was possible, because the Presidency was under a blockade and so were the bodies and organs elected by that same Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did there come a time when they ceased to function normally or at all?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. We would receive minutes from the meetings of those bodies, but if there was no quorum, then this would come in as merely an expression of their views and opinions. But in the Presidency, we did receive reports from them when there were enough members to ensure that a meeting could be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I move on to mid-July. Exhibit 328, volume 1, tab 2, Exhibit 152. The B/C/S version for Mr. Mesic. The first page of the English version on the overhead projector, please. Two questions. The first relating to this document which we can deal with shortly. This is a document, as we can see at the bottom, signed by yourself now in your position as president. You had been able to take up the Presidency. We'll come to that perhaps in a little bit, but it's signed by you in the position of president. And the decision we can see further up the page, thank you very much, says in paragraph 1: "All armed units in the SFRY territory, except JNA and regular peacetime police units, that is the police, shall be demobilised by midnight of the 18th of July." And in the margin it says: "Mesic disagrees." Can you just explain in a couple of sentences what was going on here?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, here with this decision and request was to disarm the National Guard, which was a regular composition of the Croatian police. According to legal procedure and in a legal way, this portion of the police force, like the Carabinieri, for instance, in Italy, that would be comparable, was set up, this body, this organ. It was an executive organ and it was called the Desbodna Nigarda [phoen] the National Guard Corps. And by this decision they were supposed to be disarmed, because I asked that illegal paramilitary formations be disarmed. Illegal ones, not the legal ones. I should just like to add that Croatia, for the legal organs and the National Guard Corps asked for the purchase of weapons because what they had were out-of-date. They came from a factory in Serbia, a factory that manufactured these weapons via the Federal Secretariat for the Interior. However, Croatia did not receive the okay for this. So it did legally have the right to procure weapons elsewhere if these sorts of weapons didn't exist in Yugoslavia. It was free to purchase them else where.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At about this time, was a decision made in relation to Slovenia and the pulling out of the JNA from Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what it was about. There was a military action to establish a regime along the borders of Yugoslavia and Austria, which meant that this was to be done in part of Slovenia. Slovenia had established control at certain checkpoints, border checkpoints, and in Belgrade a decision was taken to send a military contingent to set up military control along the borders. That is not something that the army -- comes under the army's competence, and the army should not have entered into this action. It was pure provocation that caused the 2.000 soldiers that had set out to establish control over the borders was not able to do anything because the Territorial Defence of Slovenia offered resistance. And I would say that this triggered off the fact that the army withdrew from Slovenia later on. And I was at the sole person at the meeting to vote against the proposal that the army withdraw from Slovenia, because I lay down conditions and said that if the Yugoslav People's Army were to withdraw both from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and other republics, then I would agree, but I would not agree that it pull out of Slovenia alone. And of course the army and Milosevic had no intention of following that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how do you regard or how did you regard that withdrawal of troops from Slovenia in connection with the disintegration of Yugoslavia more generally?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: It was quite clear to me that the withdrawal of the army from Slovenia meant the disappearance of Yugoslavia itself. And this was the further opralisation [as interpreted] of the creation of a Greater Serbia. This was repeated again and again. The people who wanted Yugoslavia to remain were in favour of this, and the Yugoslav army supported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In summary, paragraph 13 but briefly. We are still looking at particular acts and characteristics of the Presidency really itself. There came a time when the phrase "Rump Presidency" came to be used. When did that first come to be used?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army had blocked the roads in Croatia. It had blocked the airports, and I was not able to reach Belgrade. However, I was ready to convene a Presidency meeting at some other spot, some other venue, which was accessible to all the other Presidency members. And I considered that the best possible venue for that would be Brioni, the Brioni islands. And I convened a meeting on Brioni. However, the Serbian bloc resisted the idea and did not turn up. Nobody from that bloc came. And that is when we came to use a constitutional option whereby the president is not able to convene a Presidency meeting. This is then done by the vice-president. However, the Presidency could have convened a meeting, that is to say I myself could have convened a meeting but not in Belgrade as the venue. So this was an attempt to implement and affect a state coup, one which had already been carried out, in fact. But now what they were trying to do was to finish it off and that this Rump Presidency would be composed of the Serb block where Branko Kostic represented Montenegro and took over the functions of the vice-president, acting as the presiding officer and rendered decisions that which completely illegal and illegitimate. In other words, what they were introducing at that point was a state of emergency, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And roughly when did the Rump Presidency take hold? Again we'll look at this a little bit more when we look at what happened to your Presidency in detail, but when did the Rump Presidency take hold?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: It took hold approximately a month after the fact that nobody had responded to my invitation to attend the Brioni Presidency meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Along the way, because this is all in 1991 and we're passing through the summer of 1991, did the Croatian government express any views about the activation of the Supreme Command headquarters, the body you referred to not so very long ago?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both the government and the president of Croatia, Dr. Tudjman, reacted, and they did not accept the realisation of that particular plan, that is to say that the Supreme Command Headquarters be legalised because the institution itself was illegal, unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were protests or records of their position made in some way?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was recorded, and I think that those documents can be accessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Still in the summer of 1991, did you have an exchange with Kadijevic about his attitude towards the accused?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: It is interesting to note that I as the President of the Presidency of the SFRY was never able to get General Kadijevic as the Defence Minister to come to my cabinet, to my office, and have talks with me. The only time we met would be at Presidency meetings. However, I did wish the problems to be solved in a political fashion and wanted to exclude the army from the political resolution and denouement of the crisis that Yugoslavia was faced with. And so I said that I would be coming to the cabinet of the Ministry of Defence, that is to say General Kadijevic, and he did receive me on several occasions in his cabinet. When I asked him why he was doing what he was doing to the advantage of Milosevic and his plans, why he was furthering them, he said that he cannot discuss this with anyone else in Serbia because all of them were worse than Milosevic. And what I in fact said to him then was that the army was working to promote Slobodan Milosevic's plans, that is, to plot the borders of a greater Serbia. And he said expressly, "While I am alive, the Yugoslav army will protect Yugoslavia." And I said to him, "Who knows whether you will be alive because a Greater Serbia is being formed and a Greater Serbia does not need the Yugoslav army. It is being Serbicised, and it will soon be the Serb army and you won't represent one single thing in that army. You will represent nothing. "

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he challenge your characterisation of what was being done at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: No. He was persistent in wishing to convince me that the army was in fact separating the warring parties. That quite simply was not true. What the army was doing was supplying, arming, and paying all those who were attacking the institutions of Croatian power and authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were now president. We'll catch the -- we'll get the times of your Presidency shortly, but you were now president of the Presidency. Who or what was Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces under the constitution?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Under the constitution, the Supreme Commander of the armed forces was the Presidency of Yugoslavia, and the president of the Presidency was the personification of that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did Kadijevic react to any attempts that you made as president of that Presidency to intervene in the activities of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, when I persistently called for the withdrawal of the army to barracks, General Adzic as the head of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army, as well as Minister Kadijevic, did not accept this, nor did they take it into account, take much account of it. What they were doing was working along Slobodan Milosevic's arms, because the army kept becoming the Serbian army more and more. The Slovenians had stepped down, the Albanians had stepped down, the Bosniaks had stepped down. They had left. So at all practical intents and purposes it was a Serbian army under the name and guise of the Yugoslav army, whereas it was an army that was loyal exclusively to Slobodan Milosevic until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's now turn to paragraph 18 to a particular incident which happened a little earlier. The meeting at Karadjordjevo. You weren't present at that meeting. Did you have any knowledge of its being about to happen before it happened?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. As the organs of the Krajina, as it was called, continued their provocations and the representatives of the Yugoslav army, those from the KOS, the counter intelligence service, took part in all these provocations and in fact prepared, laid the ground for the army's arrival. I told Borislav Jovic, I said to him, "Why are they doing this? Why are they arming the Serbs? Because there'll be an immanent catastrophe. And if a real full-fledged war breaks out, then the 10 per cent of Serbs cannot stand up to the rest of Croatia." So what I said to him was you were cutting your nose to spite your face and working towards the disadvantage of your compatriots in Croatia. Borislav Jovic said to me, "We're not interested in Croatia. We're not interested in the Serbs in Croatia. What we are interested in is Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say the 66 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was Serb land. It was Serb land and it will remain Serb land." Now, I said, "If you're not interested in Croatian territory or the Serbs in Croatia as Croatian citizens, then let's sit down to the negotiating table and identify the problems and solve them politically. Are you in favour," I said, "That you, Tudjman, and Slobodan Milosevic sit down to the negotiating table to see what we're up against and let the problem of Bosnia be solved in the United Nations? Because Bosnia and Herzegovina is part, a constitutive element of the federation. " He said, "I agree, but I have to ask Milosevic." Some time passed and he informed me that Milosevic agreed to this but he added that anywhere in the country or outside the country that we decide to hold this meeting he would come there. I went to Zagreb, conveyed this message to President Tudjman, and he too agreed that the four of us meet. Now, as the meeting did not actually take place because Tudjman said to me, "I'll tell you when a good time for that is so you can relay this to the two in Belgrade," but Tudjman never called me and the meeting never came about, never materialised. But when I visited Zagreb, we did have a meeting in the members of the top political echelon and Tudjman said he was going to a meeting in Karadjordjevo because he wished to have a tete-a-tete meeting with Milosevic to hear what the other side wanted. So Tudjman didn't take me there, and Milosevic didn't take Borislav Jovic there. So the two of them met. Now, what they caused there is something that I cannot say with any degree of certainty, but I can say with certainty what Tudjman conveyed to us when he came back from Karadjordjevo, because we were waiting for him the entire day. Let me also emphasise one more point. Up until Karadjordjevo, Tudjman had always been in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining one entity. That was his involvement. That was his position. That was what he wanted to do for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those were his views beforehand. But after that particular meeting, he changed his opinion. He had a whole about turn in his opinion. And quite obviously Milosevic convinced him that Bosnia could be divided up. And Tudjman told us we would be getting Cazin Kladusa or, rather, the Banovina borders dating back to 1938, plus Cazin, Kladusa, and Bihac. And he said Milosevic had hold him, "Franjo, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you take Cazin, Kladusa and Bihac. That is what is called the Turkish Croatia. I don't need that. So you can have that." And then the -- this was put into practice. Fikret Abdic then proclaimed Western Bosnia as an autonomous region. We saw that on that level something was quite obviously being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move from Karadjordjevo, how soon in the press and the media was there ever any discussion of what may have happened there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Well, for quite some time the public did not know what was discussed in Karadjordjevo, but it is quite clear -- it was quite clear from what was happening in the field, on the ground, in Bosnia-Herzegovina later on the Republika Srpska was proclaimed et cetera, and on the other side the Croats proclaimed Herceg-Bosna. So that allowed one to conclude that what was in fact in play was the carving up of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC
utterances.text: Although at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
